# Dynatrace to acquire Arize in $915M AI observability deal

Mergers and Acquisitions, AI/ML

August 14, 2026

Dynatrace has agreed to acquire AI observability company Arizein a cash and stock transaction valued at $915 million, bringing AI evaluation and production observability under the same platform\. The deal is expected to close later this quarter or early in Dynatrace’s third quarter, subject to regulatory approval and other closing conditions\.

Arize focuses on monitoring and evaluating AI models, applications and agents, including detecting hallucinations, measuring output quality and tracing how AI systems behave\. Dynatrace plans to connect those capabilities with its existing visibility into applications, infrastructure, GPU usage and business processes\. That would give teams a way to follow an AI application from testing and evaluation through deployment and ongoing production monitoring\.

The acquisition also gives Dynatrace a stronger foothold with AI developers\. Arize has built its presence around AI observability and open source tools, while Dynatrace has traditionally focused on monitoring applications and infrastructure in enterprise environments\. Dynatrace said the combined platform will connect model and agent performance with application health, infrastructure data and business outcomes, while feeding production information back into AI development workflows\.

For partners and service providers, the deal adds another piece to the growing AI operations opportunity\. As customers move more AI applications and agents into production, they will need help monitoring how those systems perform, finding the source of problems and managing the infrastructure underneath them\. Bringing Arize into Dynatrace gives partners a broader set of capabilities to build AI observability and managed services around as those deployments expand\.

# Dynatrace To Buy Arize For $915 Mln In Cash, Share

Dynatrace, Inc\. \(DT\), a software intelligence and observability platform, said on Thursday that it has inked a deal to acquire Arize for $915 million in cash and stock\.

Rick McConnell, CEO of Dynatrace, said: \"Acquiring Arize advances our AI observability leadership, accelerates our roadmap, enhances our long-term growth profile, expands our reach with the developer community, and adds an incredible AI-first team to Dynatrace\.\"

Under the terms, the company will acquire Arize for $915 million, which consists of around $815 million in cash as well as replacement equity awards for Arize staff members who join Dynatrace\. Dynatrace plans to fund the acquisition through cash on hand and debt\. The transaction is expected to be closed later this quarter or early in Dynatrace's third quarter\.

The acquisition is not expected to materially impact Dynatrace's second quarter fiscal 2027 guidance or ongoing share repurchase drive\.

Post transaction, Arize's two founders, Jason Lopatecki and Aparna Dhinakaran, will join Dynatrace\. Jason will continue to lead the Arize team\.

# Dynatrace Acquires Arize: $915M Bet That AI Evaluation Starts Before Production

gettyimages\.com

Dynatrace \(NYSE: DT\) has agreed to acquire Arize, the San Francisco-based AI observability startup, in a cash-and-stock transaction valued at $915 million — the largest acquisition in the AI observability category on record\. The deal, announced August 13, 2026, is built on a specific architectural gap that every enterprise deploying AI agents has encountered but few have solved: the tools developers use to evaluate AI behavior before a system ships almost never talk to the tools that operations teams use to monitor it afterward\.

The agreement calls for approximately $815 million in cash plus replacement equity awards for Arize employees joining Dynatrace, subject to customary adjustments\. Dynatrace plans to fund the transaction through cash on hand and its existing credit facility\. The deal is expected to close later in the current fiscal quarter or early in Dynatrace's third fiscal quarter, pending standard regulatory review\.

### What Dynatrace Already Had — and What It Didn't

Before this deal, Dynatrace was not without AI observability capabilities\. In June 2026, the company open-sourced dt-evals evaluation CLI tool, a command-line tool that pulls recent production AI spans and scores them using an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation framework\. The tool includes more than ten built-in judge evaluators and statistical drift detection against a rolling baseline\. Dynatrace also traces what it calls gen\_ai spans in production — recording how LLMs behave, what they cost in token consumption, and how their output quality shifts over time\.

What it lacked was presence on the other side of the deployment boundary\.

\"Dynatrace was already shipping evaluation before this deal,\" wrote Janakiram MSV, a senior contributor at Forbes who covers cloud infrastructure, in an analysis published the day of the announcement\. \"What it did not have is a position with the AI engineers who choose an evaluation harness\. Those choices get made while an application is still being written, months before anything reaches an operations team\.\"

That is the position Arize occupies\. Arize's open-source project Phoenix — which has accumulated millions of monthly downloads and, by Arize's account, processed more than one trillion spans — gives AI engineers a free, self-hostable tracing and evaluation environment they can run on a laptop before any enterprise contract exists\. By the time an application reaches production, the instrumentation library, the trace schema, and the evaluator definitions have already been chosen\. Dynatrace is paying $815 million in cash to be in the room when that happens\.

Torsten Volk, an analyst at Omdia, explained the gap plainly in reporting by TechTarget: \"The AI observability Dynatrace already had was just focused on standard metrics, not on actually looking at model outputs in different constellations\.\"

### How Arize Evaluates What an AI Agent Actually Did

The architecture that made Arize useful — and expensive — rests on a specific telemetry model that differs meaningfully from traditional application performance monitoring\.

When a conventional application fails, the trace is diagnostic: a request entered at point A, traversed services B and C, timed out at D\. The system produced an HTTP 500 status code\. The failure is deterministic and the trace is authoritative\.

When an AI agent fails, the trace records something different\. A single agent run may involve a model request, a document retrieval step, several tool calls, and a final synthesized response\. Each operation lands as a span within a single trace\. But the output at the end is not right or wrong in the HTTP status code sense\. It may be factually incorrect while appearing fluent and confident — what the industry calls hallucination\. It may have selected the wrong tool while completing the task\. It may have stayed technically within the prompt's instructions while producing an answer that would have been corrected by any domain expert in two seconds\.

Arize addresses this with what it calls evaluators: code, human annotations, or — most commonly — another language model acting as a judge\. An evaluator applies a rubric to a span: Was the response grounded in the retrieved documents? Did the agent select the correct tool? Did it complete the assigned task? The output is a score, not a verdict\.

The critical engineering constraint this introduces — one the draft press coverage underweights — is that LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is probabilistic, not deterministic\. The evaluator model can disagree with a human reviewer\. It can drift when its underlying model version changes\. A production evaluation pipeline running LLM judges requires versioned evaluators, held-out test sets, periodic human calibration, and an explicit threshold gate before an evaluation score can block or approve a deployment\. Arize's platform provides the infrastructure for all of this; the buyer needs to understand they are adding a second AI system to their control loop, not an instrument that reports ground truth\.

Arize's Phoenix uses OpenInference as its native semantic format — its own specification for representing AI traces — rather than the OpenTelemetry generative AI semantic conventions that are emerging as the CNCF standard\. Arize AX, the commercial enterprise platform, now normalizes compatible gen\_ai attributes into OpenInference fields during ingestion, removing the need for client-side conversion\. Arize treats both conventions as first-class and expects them to converge as the OpenTelemetry specification stabilizes\. Whether they do — and which format ultimately governs the instrumentation layer for AI applications — is the unresolved standards contest this acquisition joins\. Dynatrace ranks among top OpenTelemetry contributors and now also owns the OpenInference format's primary steward\.

### The Autonomous Operations Picture

Dynatrace's deeper thesis extends beyond observability\. The company unveiled a product called Bluebox AI in 2026, designed to automate the traditional software development lifecycle — resolving incidents, preventing disruptions, and executing remediation without requiring a human in the loop for every action\. A TechTarget profile of Bluebox describes it as a new venture that \"entirely removes humans from the process,\" feeding observability and SRE agent data into coding agents throughout the development cycle\.

The Arize acquisition slots into that thesis specifically for AI agent systems\. Bluebox handles the autonomous improvement loop for conventional software\. Arize AX is designed to run an equivalent loop for AI agents: evaluating agent behavior, collecting trace data from failures, building datasets from production errors, and feeding those datasets back into iterative improvement cycles\.

\"Dynatrace has runtime telemetry; Arize can monitor, revise and refine the output quality of large language models; and Bluebox can then fix the agents based on both tools' findings,\" Volk told TechTarget on August 13\.

Mark Tomlinson, AVP of performance and observability at FreedomPay, a digital payments company currently evaluating Bluebox, offered a practitioner's view: \"DIY agents are now like websites: We're gonna have millions of them, and most of them are untested and will not scale\. Bluebox \+ Arize is a nice combination that bolsters Dynatrace's long-standing commitment to 'find and fix' value delivery\.\"

Stephen Elliot, an analyst at IDC, placed the category shift in broader context: \"Agent debugging, evaluations, agent root cause analysis and testing might even be more important than they were in the traditional software development lifecycle model, especially with agentic systems that make decisions\. I view it as a foundational investment for technology executives\.\"

### Who Arize Is

Arize was founded in 2020 by Jason Lopatecki and Aparna Dhinakaran, both UC Berkeley EECS graduates who had encountered the AI monitoring problem firsthand\. Lopatecki had built advertising systems at TubeMogul — later acquired by Adobe for over $500 million — where AI systems that broke were \"a big deal\" and no monitoring tooling existed to help diagnose them quickly\. Dhinakaran had built core machine learning infrastructure at Uber, including parts of Uber's Michelangelo ML platform, and left a Cornell computer vision PhD program to co-found Monitor ML, which Arize acquired to bring her on as co-founder\.

The company's most recent outside financing was a $70 million Series C round in February 2025, led by Adams Street Partners — itself the largest single funding round in AI observability at the time of its closing\. Strategic investors in the round included Microsoft's M12 venture fund and Datadog, one of Dynatrace's primary competitors, along with OMERS Ventures, Battery Ventures, Foundation Capital, TCV, PagerDuty, and several others\. Total venture financing across five rounds reached approximately $130 million\.

In May 2026, Arize partnered with Google Cloud to help standardize AI agent telemetry — work framing the company as a standards contributor rather than just a product vendor\. Its customer list spans both enterprise and AI-native buyers: Booking\.com, Condé Nast, Duolingo, Hyatt, PepsiCo, Priceline, TripAdvisor, Uber, and Wayfair are among those publicly named in the acquisition announcement\.

Both founders will join Dynatrace at close\. Lopatecki will continue leading the Arize team and report directly to Dynatrace CEO Rick McConnell, a structural decision that Constellation Research analysts highlighted as significant for preserving the developer community trust the acquisition is premised on\.

\"We founded Arize because AI teams needed a way to know their agents were actually working correctly, not just running,\" Lopatecki said in Dynatrace's announcement\. \"Joining Dynatrace will enable us to take that mission much further\. Together, we can bring AI evaluation and software observability into an end-to-end system\.\"

### A Category Consolidating Faster Than Buyers Expected

Dynatrace is not the only enterprise vendor moving in this direction\. In April 2026, Cisco acquired Galileo, an AI agent evaluation platform that integrates with Splunk's observability tools\. In July 2026, Harness added Agent DLC — AI agent development support — to its existing DevSecOps pipeline platform\. All three moves reflect an enterprise IT consensus the research bears out: an Omdia survey of 400 IT professionals and application developers, conducted in late 2025, found that the ability to monitor AI systems using the same observability platform already used for infrastructure ranked second on respondents' priority lists, cited as important by 49% of respondents\.

Dynatrace's deal is the largest and most expensive of these moves by a wide margin\. It also comes from the company with the most complete existing enterprise observability platform, which means the integration surface is broader and the potential value — if the technical promises hold — is higher\.

The financial terms reflect the urgency\. Dynatrace reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $555 million — up 15% year over year — with 41% organic net new ARR growth\. The Arize deal is expected to be approximately 200 basis points accretive to ARR growth for fiscal 2027, while projecting a 175-basis-point dilution to non-GAAP operating margin — a near-term trade-off the company frames as an investment in long-term platform positioning\.

McConnell framed the stakes in the announcement: \"AI is now moving into production at incredible speed, and the resulting AI Observability market opportunity is enormous\. Dynatrace anticipates customers' needs at critical inflection points, and this is one of the most significant in our history\.\"

Constellation Research captured the strategic shift Dynatrace is betting on: \"The value shifts from monitoring whether systems work to understanding whether AI decisions were right, what they changed, and whether the business improved\.\"

AI observability is projected to exceed $10 billion as a market category by 2030, according to figures in the press release\.

### One Technical Caveat Buyers Should Know

Phoenix, Arize's widely adopted open-source project, ships under the Elastic License 2\.0 rather than an Open Source Initiative-approved license\. The Elastic License 2\.0 permits broad use and self-hosting but restricts any third party from offering Phoenix itself as a managed or hosted service\. This distinction matters to the enterprise engineering community that adopted Phoenix precisely because it was not tied to a commercial contract\. What Dynatrace does with Phoenix's licensing over the coming months will be an early signal of how it handles the developer trust the acquisition is valued on\. An acquisition by a public enterprise company that then tightens an open-source license is a well-documented pattern — Elastic, Redis, HashiCorp, and MongoDB have all traveled some version of this road\. Whether Dynatrace manages the transition better is an open question\.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is AI observability and how does it differ from traditional software monitoring?

Traditional software observability tracks infrastructure health and application performance using well-defined metrics: uptime, latency, error rates, memory consumption\. These tools tell you whether a system is working\. AI observability addresses a different problem: whether the AI system's outputs are correct, relevant, and appropriate — questions that cannot be answered by an HTTP status code\. A language model that generates a plausible but factually wrong answer, selects the wrong tool in an agent pipeline, or drifts in output quality over time will appear healthy to traditional monitoring\. AI observability instruments the content of AI outputs, not just the infrastructure beneath them, using techniques like LLM-as-a-judge evaluation to score responses against rubrics for hallucination, groundedness, and task completion\.

### What is LLM-as-a-judge evaluation and why is it probabilistic?

LLM-as-a-judge evaluation uses one language model to assess the output quality of another\. The evaluator model applies a rubric — Did the response stay grounded in the retrieved documents? Did the agent select the correct tool? — and produces a score\. Unlike a conventional test that returns a deterministic pass or fail, this score reflects one model's probabilistic judgment of another model's output\. The evaluator can disagree with a human reviewer, and it can drift when its own underlying model version changes\. Running this reliably in production requires versioned evaluator definitions, held-out test sets for calibration, and explicit score thresholds before evaluation results gate deployment decisions\. Arize provides the infrastructure to manage this; the engineering discipline to use it correctly belongs to the buyer\.

### Does the Dynatrace-Arize deal close the observability gap with Datadog and Splunk?

Datadog and Splunk both have AI monitoring capabilities — Datadog traces LLM applications and supports managed LLM-as-a-judge evaluations; Splunk's AI Agent Monitoring runs both platform-side and instrumentation-side evaluations for hallucination, bias, relevance, and sentiment\. The competitive difference is where the relationship with engineering teams starts\. Datadog, Splunk, and Dynatrace all enter enterprises through operations and platform engineering\. Arize built from the opposite end: Phoenix is a free local tool that AI engineers adopt before any procurement conversation exists\. Dynatrace's bet is that by the time an application reaches production, the instrumentation and evaluator choices are already set\. Owning Arize means influencing those choices at the point where they are made\.

### Is Arize Phoenix genuinely open source?

Phoenix ships under the Elastic License 2\.0, which permits broad use, self-hosting, and modification, but restricts third parties from offering Phoenix itself as a managed or hosted service\. The Elastic License 2\.0 is not approved by the Open Source Initiative — the body that defines what \"open source\" means in formal terms\. In practice, most Phoenix users are running it self-hosted and will not encounter the restriction\. But developers who care about the formal OSI distinction, or who are evaluating long-term platform dependence, should factor the license into their decision\. How Dynatrace manages Phoenix's licensing following the close of the acquisition will be one of the clearest early signals about whether it plans to tighten the terms or maintain the current model\.

# Dynatrace Acquires AI Observability Leader Arize for $915 Million - World Today Journal

Dynatrace has signed a definitive agreement to acquire San Francisco-based AI observability startup Arize for $915 million, marking the largest corporate purchase in Dynatrace history\.

Founded in Linz, Austria, in 2005 by Bernd Greifeneder, Dynatrace currently maintains its headquarters in the greater Boston area and trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker DT\. Previous acquisitions by the software intelligence firm—including Bindplane, Metis, Runecast, and Rookout—occurred on a significantly smaller scale, with financial terms frequently remaining undisclosed\.

## Bridging the Gap in AI Software Delivery

Arize, established in 2020, offers an observability platform designed to help engineering teams test, evaluate, and monitor the behavior of machine learning models, large language models, and AI agents once deployed in production environments\. The platform helps developers detect hallucinations, measure output quality degradation, and identify data drift\. The startup has also built a strong developer following around its open-source tool, Phoenix\.

AI teams typically evaluate model behavior using isolated toolsets, while application and infrastructure engineers monitor underlying systems separately\. When an AI output fails or a user transaction stalls, identifying the root cause across that divided landscape remains challenging\. Dynatrace plans to integrate Arize to connect pre-release model evaluation directly with production monitoring, covering metrics from prompt behavior down to GPU utilization and infrastructure health\.

“AI is now moving into production at incredible speed, and the resulting AI Observability market opportunity is enormous,” Dynatrace CEO Rick McConnell stated in the company announcement\. Arize CEO Jason Lopatecki added that the combination will provide engineering organizations with AI evaluation and software observability within a single, end-to-end system\.

## Financial Impact and Market Projections

Dynatrace projects that the acquisition will add roughly 200 basis points to its annual recurring revenue growth in fiscal year 2027 while diluting non-GAAP operating margins by about 175 basis points\. The company noted that its second-quarter financial guidance and ongoing share buyback program remain unaffected by the transaction\.

Internal company projections estimate that the total addressable market for AI observability will exceed $10 billion by 2030\. Prior to the acquisition agreement, Arize had raised approximately $131 million in venture capital funding, according to data from Tracxn\. Its largest financing event was a $70 million Series C round in February 2025 led by Adams Street Partners, with participation from Microsoft venture arm M12, OMERS Ventures, Sinewave Ventures, Datadog, and PagerDuty, alongside earlier backers Foundation Capital, Battery Ventures, and TCV\.

## Transaction Timeline and Advisory Roles

The deal remains subject to regulatory review and customary closing conditions, with management anticipating completion later this quarter or early in the third fiscal quarter\. Upon closing, Arize co-founders Jason Lopatecki and Aparna Dhinakaran will transition to Dynatrace, with Lopatecki continuing to lead the Arize team and reporting directly to CEO Rick McConnell\.

Legal and financial advisory services for the transaction involved prominent Wall Street firms\. J\.P\. Morgan Securities served as exclusive financial advisor and Goodwin Procter served as legal counsel to Dynatrace\. Qatalyst Partners acted as financial advisor and DLA Piper provided legal representation to Arize\.

Dynatrace reported crossing the $2 billion threshold in annual recurring revenue for the first time in fiscal 2026, reaching $2\.054 billion—an 18 percent year-over-year increase—while employing roughly 5,600 people globally\. The company maintains its engineering headquarters in Linz, Austria, where a campus expansion project is underway to accommodate up to 1,500 developers across roughly 23,000 square metres\. Corporate officials have not yet detailed how the integration of Arize will impact staffing or operations at the Linz facility\.
